summary: This BrightQuest Treatment Centers web page explains grandiose delusions, describing them as a symptom of underlying mental health disorders in which people are convinced of their own greatness and resist correction. It covers signs and forms of these delusions, how they differ from narcissism, grandiose delusional disorder, and the rates at which bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, substance use disorders and depression produce them. It closes with an overview of residential treatment approaches, including gradual deconstruction of delusions and medication.
one_line: Overview of grandiose delusions as a symptom of underlying mental disorders, their forms, prevalence, and treatment approaches.
key_facts: Grandiose delusions are described as a symptom of an underlying mental health disorder, and people with them resist attempts to persuade them they are mistaken.
Grandiose delusions are the second most common type of delusion, trailing only persecutory delusions in incidence.
Grandiosity is defined as an exaggerated sense of self-importance.
Bipolar disorder is associated with grandiose delusions at a rate of 59-88 percent.
Schizophrenia is associated with grandiose delusions at a rate of 40-49 percent.
Substance use disorders are associated with grandiose delusions at a rate of 30 percent.
Depression is associated with grandiose delusions at a rate of 21 percent.
Only two out of every 1,000 people will be diagnosed with a delusional disorder, and about one percent of those requesting mental health treatment services will have one.
Up to 10 percent of the population will experience grandiose delusions at some point in their lives, though these are usually temporary.
Grandiose delusional disorder is one of six varieties of delusional disorder.
Delusions of grandeur are different from narcissism or egomania because they are based on false perception rather than self-serving assumptions.

Delusions associated with secondary mania can result from Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease, hypothyroidism, brain tumors, multiple sclerosis, and chronic deficiencies in B vitamins B3 and B12.
Therapists will not confront expansive delusions abruptly, instead deconstructing them gradually at a pace that won't stress the patient.
Medications used alongside therapy include antipsychotics (for schizophrenia), antidepressants (for depression), and mood-stabilizers (for bipolar disorder).
